questions.prompt: On this proton-density-weighted MRI of the knee, click the femur.
questions.hint: The long bone above the knee joint.
questions.explain: The femur is the long bone of the thigh and its condyles form the upper part of the knee joint. On proton-density imaging its marrow is intermediate to bright and its cortex is dark.

questions.prompt: On this proton-density-weighted MRI of the knee, click the tibia.
questions.hint: The larger of the two lower leg bones, below the knee joint.
questions.explain: The tibia is the weight-bearing shin bone and its plateau articulates with the femoral condyles. On proton-density imaging marrow is intermediate in signal and cortex is dark.

questions.prompt: On this proton-density-weighted MRI of the knee, click the fibula.
questions.hint: The slender lateral bone of the lower leg.
questions.explain: The fibula lies lateral to the tibia and does not bear much weight. On proton-density imaging its marrow is intermediate in signal and its cortex is dark.

questions.prompt: On this proton-density-weighted MRI of the knee, click the quadriceps femoris.
questions.hint: The large muscle group on the front of the thigh.
questions.explain: The quadriceps femoris extends the knee and attaches to the tibial tuberosity via the patellar tendon. On proton-density imaging muscle is intermediate in signal, darker than fat.

questions.prompt: A sprinter feels a sudden pull and sharp pain in the back of the thigh while accelerating. On this proton-density-weighted MRI, click the muscle group that is most likely strained.
questions.hint: It lies on the back of the thigh and flexes the knee.
questions.explain: The posterior thigh compartment contains the hamstrings, which extend the hip and flex the knee, and they are often torn during sprinting. On proton-density imaging a strain shows as feathery bright signal within the muscle.

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old falls from a ladder and lands on a straight leg; the knee swells at once and she cannot bear weight. On this proton-density-weighted MRI, click the bone whose plateau is most likely fractured.
questions.hint: The weight-bearing surface just below the knee joint.
questions.explain: Axial loading drives the femoral condyles into the tibial plateau, fracturing it, with a lipohaemarthrosis in the joint. On proton-density and fat-suppressed images the fracture line and marrow oedema are seen even when radiographs look normal.
